nodes.name: Fixed point class
nodes.statement: Let $\{x_1, \dots, x_n\}$ be the set of fixed points of $f$. We say $x_i$ and $x_j$ are in the same fixed point class if there is a path $\gamma$ from $x_i$ to $x_j$ such that $\gamma \simeq f(\gamma)$ relative $\{x_i, x_j\} =\{f(x_i), f(x_j)\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fixed points $x_i,x_j$ of $f$ are in the same class if joined by a path $\gamma$ with $\gamma\simeq f(\gamma)$ rel endpoints.

nodes.name: Free abelian group on fixed point classes
nodes.statement: This is an equivalence relation which partitions the set of fixed points into fixed point classes, and the free abelian group on fixed point classes is denoted $\mathbf{Z}[\pi_1 (X)_f]$.

nodes.name: Reidemeister trace
nodes.statement: The Reidemeister trace of $f$ is  $R(f) = \sum_{x_i} \operatorname{ind}(x_i) [x_i] \in \mathbf{Z}[\pi_1 X_f].$
nodes.statement_short: The Reidemeister trace $R(f)$ is the index-weighted sum of fixed point classes.

nodes.name: Reidemeister trace as a map of spectra
nodes.statement:
This can be resolved by recognizing that  the Reidemeister trace 
is a map of spectra 
\[
  S \to \Sigma^\infty_+ \mc{L} X^f,
\] 
where $\mc{L} X^f$ is the space of paths $x \to f(x)$ \cite{p:thesis, p:coincidence}.
conclusions:
the Reidemeister trace 
is a map of spectra
nodes.statement_short: The Reidemeister trace is a map of spectra $S\to\Sigma^\infty_+\mathcal{L}X^f$, with $\mathcal{L}X^f$ the space of paths $x\to f(x)$.

nodes.name: Folk theorem: Euler characteristic via cyclotomic trace
nodes.statement_short: The composite $S\to K(\Sigma^\infty_+\Omega X)\to THH\simeq\Sigma^\infty_+\mathcal{L}X\to S$ of $[X]$ with the cyclotomic trace is the Euler characteristic.

nodes.name: Reidemeister trace as THH transfer
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a topological space homotopy equivalent to a finite CW-complex. The Reidemeister trace is naturally equivalent to the $\thh$ transfer \[ \thh(\operatorname{Mod}^c_S) \to \thh(\operatorname{Mod}^c_{\Sigma^\infty_+ \Omega X})\to \thh(\operatorname{Mod}^c_{\Sigma^\infty_+ \Omega X}; F). \]
assumptions: Let $X$ be a topological space homotopy equivalent to a finite CW-complex.
conclusions: The Reidemeister trace is naturally equivalent to the $\thh$ transfer
nodes.statement_short: For $X$ a finite CW-complex up to homotopy, the Reidemeister trace equals the twisted THH transfer.
nodes.label: thm:lm_generalization

nodes.name: Category of compact modules
nodes.statement: In this statement $\operatorname{Mod}^c_A$ is the category of compact $A$ modules.

nodes.name: Class [f] of an endomorphism in pi_0 THH
nodes.statement:
For a ring spectrum $A$, an endomorphism $f\colon M \to M$ of a compact $A$-module spectrum determines a map 
$S\to \operatorname{End}(M) $.  Composing with the inclusion of the zero skeleton defines a map 
\[
  S\to \operatorname{End}(M) \to \thh(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A) 
\]
and so an element $[f] \in \pi_0 \thh(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A)$.
nodes.statement_short: An endomorphism $f$ of a compact $A$-module gives $S\to\mathrm{End}(M)\to THH(\mathrm{Mod}^c_A)$, hence $[f]\in\pi_0 THH(\mathrm{Mod}^c_A)$.

nodes.name: Morita image of [f] is the bicategorical trace
nodes.statement: The image of $[f] \in \pi_0 \thh(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A)$ under the Morita invariance isomorphism \[ \thh(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A) \simeq \thh(A) \] is the bicategorical trace of $f$. In particular, for a module $M \in \operatorname{Mod}^c_A$, the image of $[\operatorname{id}_M]$ is $\chi(M)$.
assumptions: an endomorphism $f\colon M \to M$ of a compact $A$-module spectrum
nodes.statement_short: Under Morita invariance $THH(\mathrm{Mod}^c_A)\simeq THH(A)$, $[f]$ maps to the bicategorical trace of $f$; $[\mathrm{id}_M]$ maps to $\chi(M)$.
nodes.label: thm:what_happens_on_pi

nodes.name: Bicategory
nodes.statement: A {\bf bicategory} $\mc{B}$ consists of objects, $A, B, \ldots$, called $0$-cells,  and categories $\mc{B}(A, B)$ for each pair of objects $A, B$.

nodes.name: 1-cells and 2-cells
nodes.statement: Objects in the category $\mc{B}(A, B)$ are called 1-cells and morphisms are called 2-cells.

nodes.name: Unit 1-cell
nodes.statement: The unit $1$-cell associated to a 0-cell $A$ is denoted $U_A$.

nodes.name: Horizontal composition
nodes.statement:
There are horizontal composition functors
\[
\odot \colon  \mc{B}(A, B) \times \mc{B}(B, C) \to \mc{B}(A, C). 
\]
They need not be strictly associative or unital.

nodes.name: Bimodule and parametrized-space bicategories
nodes.statement_short: Rings with bimodules (tensor product), and spaces with spaces over products (pullback), are the guiding bicategories.

nodes.name: Pointwise cofibrant spectral category
nodes.statement: A spectral category $\mc{C}$ is \textbf{pointwise cofibrant} if each mapping spectrum $\mc{C}(a, b)$ is cofibrant in the enriching category.
differentia: each mapping spectrum $\mc{C}(a, b)$ is cofibrant in the enriching category

nodes.name: Module over a spectral category
nodes.statement: Let $\mc{C}$ be a spectral category. Then a $\mc{C}$\textbf{-module} is a spectral functor $\mc{C} \to \operatorname{Sp}$.

nodes.name: Bimodule over spectral categories
nodes.statement: A \textbf{$(\mc{C}, \mc{D})$-bimodule} is a functor $\mc{M}\colon \mc{C}^{\text{op}} \sma \mc{D} \to \operatorname{Sp}$. That is, $\mc{M}$ is a collection of spectra $\mc{M}(c, d)$ for $c \in \mc{C}$, $d \in \mc{D}$ together with maps \begin{align*} &\mc{C}(c, c') \sma \mc{M}(c', d) \to \mc{M}(c, d)\\ &\mc{M}(c, d) \sma \mc{D}(d,d') \to \mc{M}(c, d') \end{align*} An $(\mc{C}, \mc{D})$-bimodule is {\bf pointwise cofibrant} if $\mc{M}(c, d)$ is cofibrant. A {\bf morphism} of $(\mc{C}, \mc{D})$-bimodules $\mc{M} \to \mc{M}'$ is a collection of maps $\mc{M}(c, d) \to \mc{M}'(c, d)$ which commute with the appropriate structure.
nodes.statement_short: A $(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})$-bimodule is a spectral functor $\mathcal{C}^{op}\wedge\mathcal{D}\to Sp$; also pointwise cofibrancy and morphisms.

nodes.name: Opposite variance convention
nodes.statement: Note that this has the opposite variance of what is standard for bimodules in the literature. This convention seems to be more useful for bookkeeping for us.

nodes.name: Topological Hochschild homology with coefficients
nodes.statement: Let $\mc{C}$ be a pointwise cofibrant spectral category, and $\mc{Q}$ a $(\mc{C},\mc{C})$-bimodule. The \textbf{topological Hochschild homology of $\mc{C}$ with coefficients in $\mc{Q}$} is the geometric realization of a spectrum whose $n$th simplicial level is \[ \thh(\mc{C}; \mc{Q})_n \coloneqq N^{\text{cy}}_n (\mc{C}, \mc{Q}) = \bigvee_{c_0, \dots, c_n} \mc{C}(c_0, c_1) \sma \mc{C}(c_1, c_2) \sma \cdots \sma \mc{C}(c_{n-1}, c_n) \sma \mc{Q}(c_n, c_0) \] That is, \[ \thh(\mc{C};\mc{Q}) \coloneqq \vert\thh(\mc{C};\mc{Q})_\bullet\vert \]
nodes.definiendum: topological Hochschild homology of $\mc{C}$ with coefficients in $\mc{Q}$
nodes.statement_short: $THH(\mathcal{C};\mathcal{Q})$ is the realization of the cyclic nerve $\bigvee \mathcal{C}(c_0,c_1)\wedge\cdots\wedge\mathcal{Q}(c_n,c_0)$.

nodes.name: Bokstedt construction vs cyclic nerve
nodes.statement: The reader is warned that most literature makes a distinction between B\"{o}kstedt's construction $\thh(\mc{C};\mc{Q})$ and $N^{\text{cy}}(\mc{C};\mc{Q})$. When $\mc{C}$ is pointwise cofibrant, they are equivalent. Since we will work on the level of homotopy categories, and ignore questions of equivariance, we therefore ignore the distinction.

nodes.name: Base change bimodule _F C_G
nodes.statement: Let $F\colon \mc{A} \to \mc{C}$ and $G\colon \mc{B} \to \mc{C}$ be functors between spectral categories. Define an $(\mc{A}, \mc{B})$-bimodule $ \ _F \mc{C}_G$ as follows. For objects $a\in \mc{A}$ and $b \in \mc{B}$ \[ \ _F \mc{C}_G (a, b) \coloneqq \mc{C}(F(a), G(b)). \] The right action of $\mc{B}$ on $\ _F \mc{C}_G$ is given by the functor $G$: \begin{align*} \ _F \mc{C}_G(a, b) \sma \mc{B} (b, b') &= \mc{C}(F(a),G(b)) \sma \mc{B} (b, b') \to \mc{C}(F(a), G(b)) \sma \mc{C}(G(b), G(b'))\\ &\to \mc{C} (F(a), G(b')) = \ _F \mc{C}_G (a, b') \end{align*} The left action of $\mc{A}$ is similar.
nodes.statement_short: For functors $F,G$ into $\mathcal{C}$, ${}_F\mathcal{C}_G(a,b)=\mathcal{C}(F(a),G(b))$ with actions through $F$ and $G$.
nodes.label: def:base_change

nodes.name: Endofunctor base change
nodes.statement: When $F\colon \mc{C} \to \mc{C}$ is an endofunctor and $G = \id$, we can form $\ _F \mc{C}$, and similarly $\mc{C}_F$.

nodes.name: Right twisted topological Hochschild homology
nodes.statement: Let $\mc{C}$ be a pointwise cofibrant spectral category and $F\colon \mc{C} \to \mc{C}$ be an endofunctor. We defined the \textbf{right twisted topological Hochschild homology} to be \[ \thh(\mc{C}; F)\coloneqq\thh(\mc{C}; \mc{C}_F) \]
nodes.label: right_twisted

nodes.name: Untwisted case
nodes.statement: When $F = \id$, we recover $\thh(\mc{C})$.

nodes.name: Twisted THH of compact modules
nodes.statement: A good example to keep in mind is the following. Let $A$ be a commutative ring spectrum, $P$ be an $A$-module, and let $\operatorname{Mod}^c_A$ denote the category of compact $A$-modules. Consider the functor $-\wedge_AP \colon \operatorname{Mod}^c_A \to \operatorname{Mod}^c_A$ given by $M \mapsto M \sma_A P$, where $M \in \operatorname{Mod}^c_A$. We show in \cref{ex:twist_thh_morita} that the twisted $\thh(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A; -\wedge _AP)$ coincides with $\thh(A; P)$.
nodes.statement_short: For commutative $A$ and $A$-module $P$, twisted $THH(\mathrm{Mod}^c_A;-\wedge_AP)$ agrees with $THH(A;P)$.
nodes.label: eg:twisted_thh

nodes.name: Functoriality of THH
nodes.statement:
Topological Hochschild homology is clearly functorial in the bimodule coordinate so that given a map of $(\mc{C}, \mc{C})$-bimodules $\mc{Q} \to \mc{Q}'$  there is a map
\[
\thh(\mc{C}; \mc{Q}) \to \thh(\mc{C}; \mc{Q}').  
\]
Furthermore, if $\mc{A} \to \mc{C}$ is a map, then we get an induced map $\thh(\mc{A}) \to \thh(\mc{C})$.
assumptions: given a map of $(\mc{C}, \mc{C})$-bimodules $\mc{Q} \to \mc{Q}'$
if $\mc{A} \to \mc{C}$ is a map
given a map of $(\mc{C}, \mc{C})$-bimodules $\mc{Q} \to \mc{Q}'$
if $\mc{A} \to \mc{C}$ is a map

nodes.name: Blumberg-Mandell functoriality refinement
nodes.statement:
There is also a refinement of both \cite{blumberg_mandell}. Let $F\colon  \mc{A} \to \mc{C}$ be a map of spectral categories and let $\mc{Q}$ be a $(\mc{C},\mc{C})$-bimodule. Then there is a map
\[
\thh(\mc{A};{_F\mc{Q}_F}) \to \thh(\mc{C}, \mc{Q}) 
\]
and if there is a map $\mc{P} \to {_F \mc{Q}_F}$ we obtain
\[
\thh(\mc{A}; \mc{P}) \to \thh (\mc{C}, \mc{Q}). 
\]
assumptions: Let $F\colon  \mc{A} \to \mc{C}$ be a map of spectral categories and let $\mc{Q}$ be a $(\mc{C},\mc{C})$-bimodule.
nodes.statement_short: A spectral functor $F$ and bimodule $\mathcal{Q}$ give $THH(\mathcal{A};{}_F\mathcal{Q}_F)\to THH(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{Q})$, and similarly for $\mathcal{P}\to{}_F\mathcal{Q}_F$.

nodes.name: Model structure on bimodules
nodes.statement: The category, $\operatorname{Mod}_{(\mc{C}, \mc{D})}$ of $(\mc{C}, \mc{D})$-bimodules forms a closed model category with object-wise weak equivalences.
conclusions: forms a closed model category with object-wise weak equivalences

nodes.name: Pointwise cofibrant replacement of spectral categories
nodes.statement: Given a small spectral category $\mc{C}$ there is an endofunctor $Q\colon \mc{C}\text{at}_{Sp} \to \mc{C}\text{at}_{Sp}$ such that $Q \mc{C}$ is pointwise cofibrant and there is a map $Q \mc{C} \to \mc{C}$ that is a pointwise weak equivalence. Furthermore, if $\mc{M}$ is a cofibrant $(\mc{C}, \mc{D})$-module, then $\mc{M}$ is pointwise cofibrant.
assumptions: Given a small spectral category $\mc{C}$
conclusions: if $\mc{M}$ is a cofibrant $(\mc{C}, \mc{D})$-module, then $\mc{M}$ is pointwise cofibrant

nodes.name: THH preserves weak equivalences in the coefficient
nodes.statement:
Furthermore, by the remark following \cite[Prop.~3.6]{blumberg_mandell}, if $\mc{C}$ is pointwise cofibrant, and $\mc{P} \to \mc{P}'$ is a weak equivalence of spectral categories,
 then the induced map 
 \[
	\thh(\mc{C}, \mc{P}) \to \thh (\mc{C}, \mc{P}')
 \]
is a weak equivalence.
assumptions: if $\mc{C}$ is pointwise cofibrant, and $\mc{P} \to \mc{P}'$ is a weak equivalence of spectral categories

nodes.name: Bicategory of small spectral categories
nodes.statement: The bicategory of small spectral categories is the bicategory whose objects are pointwise cofibrant small spectral categories, and whose morphism categories are \[ \operatorname{Ho}\left(\operatorname{Mod}_{(\mc{C}, \mc{D})}\right) \] for pointwise cofibrant small spectral categories $\mc{C}$ and $\mc{D}$.

nodes.name: Composition of bimodules via bar construction
nodes.statement: The composition of 1-cells is defined as follows. Let $\mc{M}$ be an $(\mc{C}, \mc{D})$-bimodule and $\mc{N}$ an $(\mc{D},\mc{E})$-bimodule. Then we may form an $(\mc{C}, \mc{E})$-bimodule $\mc{M} \odot \mc{N}$ \begin{align*} (\mc{M} \odot \mc{N})(c,e) &\coloneqq \mc{M}(c,-) \sma^{\mathbf{L}}_{\mc{D}} \mc{N}(-,e)\\ &\coloneqq B(\mc{M}(c,-), \mc{D}, \mc{N}(-,e)) \end{align*} where $B(-,-,-)$ denotes the two-sided bar construction. This descends to \[ \operatorname{Ho}\left(\Mod_{(\mc{C}, \mc{D})}\right) \times \operatorname{Ho}\left(\Mod_{(\mc{D}, \mc{E})}\right) \to \operatorname{Ho}\left(\Mod_{(\mc{C}, \mc{E})}\right) \] Checking that this is associative is straightforward but tedious. One explicitly writes out the bar construction and cofibrantly replaces as needed. The composition of 2-cells is the composition of natural transformations.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{M}\odot\mathcal{N}$ is the derived tensor (two-sided bar construction) over $\mathcal{D}$; it descends to homotopy categories.

nodes.name: Shadow functor
nodes.statement: Let $\mc{B}$ be a bicategory. A \textbf{shadow functor} for $\mc{B}$ consists of functors \[ \shvar{}{-}\colon \mc{B}(C,C) \to \mathbf{T} \] for each object $C$ of $\mc{B}$ and some fixed category $\mathbf{T}$, equipped with a natural isomorphism \[ \theta\colon \shvar{}{M\odot N}\xrightarrow{\cong} \shvar{}{N\odot M} \] for $M\in \mc{B}(C, D)$ and $N\in \mc{B}(D, C)$ such that the following diagrams commute whenever they make sense: \[\xymatrix{ \shvar{}{(M\odot N)\odot P} \ar[r]^\theta \ar[d]_{\shvar{}{a}} & \shvar{}{P \odot (M\odot N)} \ar[r]^{\shvar{}{a}} & \shvar{}{(P\odot M) \odot N} \\ \shvar{}{M\odot (N\odot P)} \ar[r]^\theta & \shvar{}{(N\odot P)\odot M} \ar[r]^{\shvar{}{a}} & \shvar{}{N\odot (P\odot M)}\ar[u]_\theta }\] \[\xymatrix{ \shvar{}{M\odot U_C} \ar[r]^\theta \ar[dr]_{\shvar{}{r}} & \shvar{}{U_C\odot M} \ar[d]^{\shvar{}{l}} \ar[r]^\theta & \shvar{}{M\odot U_C} \ar[dl]^{\shvar{}{r}} \\ &\shvar{}{M}}\]
nodes.statement_short: A shadow on $\mathcal{B}$ is functors $\langle\!\langle-\rangle\!\rangle$ on endo-1-cells with a natural cyclic isomorphism $\theta$ compatible with associator and unitors.
nodes.label: def:shadow

nodes.name: Shadow twist squared is identity
assumptions: if $\shvar{}{-}$ is a shadow functor on $\mc{B}$

nodes.name: THH is a shadow
nodes.statement: Topological Hochschild Homology is a shadow. That is, it gives a family of functors \[ \thh (-) \colon \operatorname{Ho}\left(\operatorname{Mod}_{(\mc{C}, \mc{C})}\right) \to \operatorname{Ho}(\operatorname{Sp}) \] that satisfy the required properties.
conclusions: Topological Hochschild Homology is a shadow.
nodes.label: thm:thh_shadow

nodes.name: Proof that THH is a shadow
nodes.statement: The main property of shadows is that for $(\mc{C}, \mc{D})$-bimodule $\mc{M}$ and a $(\mc{D}, \mc{C})$-bimodule $\mc{N}$, there is an isomorphism \[ \theta \colon \shvar{}{\mc{M} \odot \mc{N}} \to \shvar{}{\mc{N} \odot \mc{M}}. \] Unpacking this into the usual notation, this is equivalent to the demand that there is an isomorphism \[ \theta\colon \thh (\mc{C}, B(\mc{M}, \mc{D}, \mc{N})) \to \thh(\mc{D}, B(\mc{N}, \mc{C}, \mc{M})) \] However, this is the classical Dennis-Morita-Waldhausen argument \cite[Prop.~6.2]{blumberg_mandell} --- in this case, there is an isomorphism of underlying point-set spectra. The commutativity of the rest of the diagrams follow from essentially the same argument.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce the shadow isomorphism to the Dennis-Morita-Waldhausen isomorphism of cyclic bar constructions.

nodes.name: Key shadow property
nodes.statement: The main property of shadows is that for $(\mc{C}, \mc{D})$-bimodule $\mc{M}$ and a $(\mc{D}, \mc{C})$-bimodule $\mc{N}$, there is an isomorphism \[ \theta \colon \shvar{}{\mc{M} \odot \mc{N}} \to \shvar{}{\mc{N} \odot \mc{M}}. \]
nodes.statement_short: State the required cyclic isomorphism $\theta$.

nodes.name: Dennis-Morita-Waldhausen
nodes.statement: Unpacking this into the usual notation, this is equivalent to the demand that there is an isomorphism \[ \theta\colon \thh (\mc{C}, B(\mc{M}, \mc{D}, \mc{N})) \to \thh(\mc{D}, B(\mc{N}, \mc{C}, \mc{M})) \] However, this is the classical Dennis-Morita-Waldhausen argument \cite[Prop.~6.2]{blumberg_mandell} --- in this case, there is an isomorphism of underlying point-set spectra. The commutativity of the rest of the diagrams follow from essentially the same argument.
nodes.statement_short: Unpack to THH of bar constructions and apply the Dennis-Morita-Waldhausen isomorphism; diagrams similarly.

nodes.name: Bicategory of monoids and bimodules
nodes.statement: Let $\mc{B}(\mathbf{Mon}(\mc{V}))$ be the bicategory whose  objects are monoids in $\mc{V}$, 1-cells are bimodules over monoids in $\mc{V}$ and whose 2-cells are maps of bimodules.

nodes.name: Bicategory of enriched categories and bimodules
nodes.statement: Let $\mc{B}(\mathbf{Cat}(\mc{V}))$ be the bicategory whose objects are categories enriched in $\mc{V}$, whose 1-cells are functors $F \colon  \mc{C}^{\text{op}} \otimes \mc{D} \to \mc{V}$ (also known as $(\mc{C}, \mc{D})$-bimodules) and whose 2-cells are natural transformations of such.

nodes.name: Bicategory of spectral categories
nodes.statement: Let $\mc{V} = \mathbf{Sp}$. Then $\mc{B}(\mathbf{Cat}(\mc{V}))$ is the bicategory of spectral categories. Because of the homotopical issues outlined above we work in the full subcategory of pointwise cofibrant small spectral categories. In general, if $\mc{V}$ and $\mathbf{Cat}(\mc{V})$ have some kind of homotopical structure, we understand $\mc{B}(\mathbf{Cat}(\mc{V}))$ to be modified in order to give the homotopically correct definitions.
nodes.label: bcat_example

nodes.name: Embedding of monoids into categories
nodes.statement: Note that every monoid in $\mc{V}$ can be made into a $\mc{V}$-category with one object, giving an embedding $\mathbf{Mon}(\mc{V}) \to \mathbf{Cat}(\mc{V})$; this is the enriched version of the usual embedding $\mathbf{Mon} \to \mathbf{Cat}$. Thus, at the level of bicategories, we have an embedding \[ \mc{B}(\mathbf{Mon}(\mc{V})) \to \mc{B}(\mathbf{Cat}(\mc{V})). \]

nodes.name: Dual pair
nodes.statement: We say that a 1-cell $M\in \mc{B}(C,D)$ in a bicategory is \textbf{right dualizable} if there is a 1-cell $N\in \mc{B}(D,C)$, called its \textbf{right dual}, and coevaluation and evaluation 2-cells $\eta\colon U_C \to M\odot N$ and $\epsilon \colon N\odot M\to U_D$ satisfying the triangle identities. We say that $(M,N)$ is a \textbf{dual pair}, that $N$ is \textbf{left dualizable}, and that $M$ is its \textbf{left dual}.
nodes.statement_short: $M$ is right dualizable with right dual $N$ if there are $\eta: U_C\to M\odot N$ and $\epsilon: N\odot M\to U_D$ satisfying triangle identities.

nodes.name: Pasting diagram conventions
nodes.statement: While we will not use them as a formal proof, some of the results in the next sections have illuminating graphical descriptions as pasting diagrams. In our pasting diagrams vertices represent 0-cells, edges represent 1-cells, and colored regions represent 2-cells. Since we will need to eventually make circular diagrams (\cref{fig:pasting_trace}), we do not identify 0-cells when they are the same. Instead we rely on the convention that vertices in consecutive layers that align should be regarded as the same. We suppress unit isomorphisms and many unit 1-cells. Pale gray regions are identity 2-cells. See \cref{fig;dual_pairs} for pasting diagrams for a dual pair.

nodes.name: Dualizable bimodules over rings
nodes.statement: For rings $C$ and $D$, an $(C,D)$-bimodule $M$ is right dualizable if it is finitely generated and projective as a right $D$-module. A choice of dual is the $(D,C)$-bimodule of right $D$-module homomorphisms $\Hom_D(M,D)$. Note that $\Hom_D(M,D)$ is regarded as a $(D,C)$-bimodule using the left $C$-module structure on $M$ and left $D$-module structure on $D$. The coevaluation map is the composite \[ C\to \Hom_D(M,M)\xleftarrow{\sim} M\otimes_D\Hom_D(M,D) \] where the second map is an isomorphism since $M$ is finitely generated and projective as an $D$ module. The evaluation map for this dual pair is the evaluation map \[ \Hom_D(M,D)\otimes_C M\to D. \] Dually, $M$ is left dualizable if it is finitely generated and projective as a left $C$-module.

nodes.name: Costenoble-Waner duality
nodes.statement: Costenoble-Waner duality \cite[Chapter~18]{maysig:pht} is a special case of the duality theory above and generalizes Spanier-Whitehead and Atiyah duality. The parameterized stable homotopy category $\operatorname{Ex}$ of \cite{maysig:pht} has a fiberwise suspension spectrum functor from the bicategory of fibered spaces (without sections). If we regard a closed smooth manifold $X$, or compact ENR, as a space over $\ast\times X$ its fiberwise suspension spectrum is dualizable with dual the desuspension of the fiberwise one point compactification of the normal bundle \cite[18.5.1]{maysig:pht}.

nodes.name: Bicategorical trace
nodes.statement: \cite{p:thesis} Let $\mc{B}$ be a bicategory with a shadow functor and $(M,N)$ be a dual pair. The \textbf{trace} of a 2-cell $f\colon Q\odot M\rightarrow M\odot P$ is the composite: \[ \shvar{}{Q}\cong \shvar{}{Q\odot U_C}\xrightarrow{\shvar{}{\id_Q\odot\eta}} \shvar{}{Q\odot M\odot N} \xrightarrow{\shvar{}{f\odot\id_N}} \shvar{}{M\odot P\odot N} \xrightarrow{\theta} \shvar{}{N\odot M\odot P} \xrightarrow{\shvar{}{\epsilon \odot \id_P}} \shvar{}{U_D\odot P}\cong \shvar{}{P}. \] The trace of a 2-cell $g\colon N\odot Q\to P\odot N$ is \[ \shvar{}{Q}\cong \shvar{}{U_C\odot Q}\xrightarrow{\shvar{}{\eta\odot\id_Q}} \shvar{}{M\odot N\odot Q} \xrightarrow{\shvar{}{\id_M\odot g}} \shvar{}{M\odot P\odot N} \xrightarrow{\theta} \shvar{}{P\odot N\odot M} \xrightarrow{\shvar{}{\id_P \odot \epsilon}} \shvar{}{P\odot U_D}\cong \shvar{}{P}. \]
nodes.statement_short: The trace of $f: Q\odot M\to M\odot P$ is the composite on shadows of coevaluation, $f$, the cyclic twist $\theta$, and evaluation.
nodes.label: defn:trace

nodes.name: Bullseye diagrams for traces
nodes.statement: After applying the shadow, we glue together vertical edges to form a bullseye diagram as in \cref{fig:pasting_trace}. As above, we do collapse most 0-cells. In these diagrams we read 2-cells as directed from the innermost circle to the outermost circle and 1-cells clockwise. Once we have applied the shadow we compose 2-cells by stacking circles.

nodes.name: Dold-Puppe functoriality of trace
nodes.statement: In \cite{dold_puppe}, there is a particularly elegant proof of the Lefschetz fixed point theorem that relies on the observations that the fixed point index \cite{dold_idx} is the trace in the stable homotopy category, the Lefschetz number is the trace in the homotopy category of chain complexes, and the symmetric monoidal trace is functorial: that is \[ F(\mathrm{tr}(f))=\mathrm{tr}(F(f)). \] The Reidemeister trace, in its many variants, is an example of the bicategorical trace \cite{p:thesis}. Since these are bicategorical traces, the identification of the varied forms of the Reidemeister trace is a consequence of the functoriality of the bicategorical trace.

nodes.name: Notation for twisted coevaluation and evaluation
nodes.statement:
Let $(M,N)$ be a dual pair and $Q$ and $P$ be 1-cells so that $N\odot Q\odot M$ and $M\odot P\odot N$ are defined. We then  fix the following notation: 
\begin{gather*}
  \rsm{\eta}{M}{N}{Q}\colon Q\odot M\cong U_C\odot Q\odot M
  \xrightarrow{\eta\odot \id_Q\odot \id_M} 
  M\odot N\odot Q\odot M
 \\
  \rsm{\epsilon}{M}{N}{P}\colon M\odot P\odot N\odot M
  \xrightarrow{\id_M \odot \id_P \odot\epsilon}
  M\odot P\odot U_D\cong M\odot P
 \\
   \lsm{\eta}{M}{N}{Q} \colon N\odot Q\cong N\odot Q\odot U_C
  \xrightarrow{\id_N\odot \id_Q\odot \eta} N\odot Q\odot M\odot N
 \\
   \lsm{\epsilon}{M}{N}{P}\colon N\odot M\odot P\odot N
   \xrightarrow{\epsilon\odot \id_P \odot \id_N }
   U_D\odot P\odot N\cong P\odot N
\end{gather*}
nodes.statement_short: Notation for coevaluation/evaluation 2-cells tensored with identities on $Q$, $P$, $M$, $N$.

nodes.name: Dual of a 2-cell and its trace
nodes.statement: If $(M,N)$ is a dual pair, the {\bf dual} of a map $g\colon N\odot Q\to P\odot N$, denoted $g^\star$, is the composite \begin{align*} Q\odot M\xrightarrow{\rsm{\eta}{M}{N}{Q}} M\odot N\odot Q\odot M\xrightarrow{\id_M \odot g\odot \id_M}M\odot P\odot N\odot M \xrightarrow{\rsm{\epsilon}{M}{N}{P} } M\odot P \end{align*} Since $\mathrm{tr}(g)=\mathrm{tr}(g^\star)$ \cite[Prop.~7.6]{ps:bicat} we freely move between traces defined with respect to $M$ and those defined with respect to $N$. Note that $\rsm{\eta}{M}{N}{Q}$ is the dual of $\lsm{\eta}{M}{N}{Q}$, $\rsm{\epsilon}{M}{N}{Q}$ is the dual of $\lsm{\epsilon}{M}{N}{Q}$, and \begin{gather*} \shvar{}{Q}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{tr}\left(\rsm{\eta}{M}{N}{Q}\right)=\mathrm{tr}\left(\lsm{\eta}{M}{N}{Q}\right)} \shvar{}{N\odot Q\odot M} \quad \text{and } \quad \shvar{}{M\odot P\odot N}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{tr}\left(\rsm{\epsilon}{M}{N}{P}\right)=\mathrm{tr}\left(\lsm{\epsilon}{M}{N}{P}\right)} \shvar{}{P} \end{gather*}
nodes.statement_short: Defines the dual $g^\star$ of $g: N\odot Q\to P\odot N$; $\mathrm{tr}(g)=\mathrm{tr}(g^\star)$, so traces w.r.t. $M$ or $N$ agree.
nodes.label: left_or_right_for_trace

nodes.name: Simplified traces of twisted coevaluation and evaluation
nodes.statement: For a dual pair $(M,N)$ and 1-cells $Q$ and $P$ so that $N\odot Q\odot M$ and $M\odot P\odot N$ are defined, $\mathrm{tr}\left(\rsm{\epsilon}MNP\right)$ is \[ \shvar{}{M\odot P\odot N}\xrightarrow{\sim}\shvar{}{P\odot N\odot M}\xrightarrow{\shvar{}{\id_P\odot \epsilon}} \shvar{}{P\odot U_D}\cong\shvar{}{P} \] and $\mathrm{tr}\left(\rsm{\eta}MNQ\right)$ is the composite \[ \shvar{}{Q}\cong \shvar{}{Q\odot U_C}\xrightarrow{\shvar{}{\id_Q\odot \eta}}\shvar{}{Q\odot M\odot N}\cong \shvar{}{N\odot Q\odot M}. \]
assumptions: For a dual pair $(M,N)$ and 1-cells $Q$ and $P$ so that $N\odot Q\odot M$ and $M\odot P\odot N$ are defined
nodes.statement_short: The traces of $\eta^{(M,N)}_Q$ and $\epsilon^{(M,N)}_P$ reduce to a cyclic twist composed with a single evaluation or coevaluation.
nodes.label: rsm_simplified

nodes.name: Proof of simplified traces
nodes.statement: In the trace of $\rsm{\epsilon}{M}{N}{P}$ (\cref{fig:morita_trace}) there is a coevaluation/evaluation pair that can be canceled. Cancelling this pair gives the composite above and is illustrated in \cref{fig:morita_trace_2}. The proof for $\rsm{\eta}MNQ$ is similar.
nodes.statement_short: Cancel a coevaluation/evaluation pair in the pasting diagram of the trace.

nodes.name: Locate cancelling pair
nodes.statement: In the trace of $\rsm{\epsilon}{M}{N}{P}$ (\cref{fig:morita_trace}) there is a coevaluation/evaluation pair that can be canceled.
nodes.statement_short: Observe a coevaluation/evaluation pair in the trace diagram.

nodes.name: Cancel and conclude
nodes.statement: Cancelling this pair gives the composite above and is illustrated in \cref{fig:morita_trace_2}. The proof for $\rsm{\eta}MNQ$ is similar.
nodes.statement_short: Cancelling it gives the stated composite; the other case is similar.

nodes.name: Trace of identity is the Euler characteristic
nodes.statement:
The stable homotopy category is symmetric monoidal and the suspension spectrum of a closed smooth manifold or compact ENR $X$ is dualizable.   The trace of the identity map 
of $X$ is a stable map $S\to S$ and this is the Euler characteristic of $X$ under the identification of stable $\pi_0$ with $\mathbb{Z}$.
assumptions: the suspension spectrum of a closed smooth manifold or compact ENR $X$ is dualizable
conclusions: this is the Euler characteristic of $X$ under the identification of stable $\pi_0$ with $\mathbb{Z}$

nodes.name: Euler characteristic of a dualizable 1-cell
nodes.statement: If $M\in \mc{B}(C,D)$ and $M$ is right dualizable, the \textbf{Euler characteristic} (\cref{fig:euler_char}) is the trace of the identity 2-cell of $M$ and is a map \[\shvar{}{U_C}\to \shvar{}{U_D}.\] If $N$ is the right dual of $M$, $\chi(M)=\chi(N)$.
also_stated_at:
As a result, we refer to symmetric monoidal traces
of identity maps and bicategorical traces of identity 2-cells as {\bf Euler characteristics} and denote them by $\chi(X)$.
nodes.label: defn:euler_characteristic

nodes.name: Euler characteristic as a map
nodes.statement: Thinking of the Euler characteristic as a \textit{map} rather than a \textit{object} is an important psychological move for working with constructions in the sequel. The importance of this formulation of the Euler characteristic cannot be overstated.

nodes.name: Trace of a composite of dual pairs
nodes.statement: \cite[16.5.1]{maysig:pht}\cite[Prop.~7.5]{ps:bicat} If $M_1\in \mc{B}(C,D)$ and $M_2\in \mc{B}(D,E)$ are right dualizable, then $M_1\odot M_2$ is right dualizable. The trace of \[ Q_1\odot M_1\odot M_2\xrightarrow{f_1\odot \id_{M_2}} M_1\odot Q_2\odot M_2\xrightarrow{\id_{M_1}\odot f_2} M_1\odot M_2\odot Q_3 \] is \[ \shvar{}{Q_1}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{tr}(f_1)}\shvar{}{Q_2}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{tr}(f_2)}\shvar{}{Q_3}. \]
assumptions: If $M_1\in \mc{B}(C,D)$ and $M_2\in \mc{B}(D,E)$ are right dualizable
nodes.statement_short: Composites of right dualizable 1-cells are dualizable and the trace of a composite 2-cell is the composite of traces.
nodes.label: lem:composite_dual_pair

nodes.name: Twisted composite M1 odot f odot M2
nodes.statement:
Given dual pairs $(M_1,N_1)$ and $(M_2, N_2)$, a 1-cell $L$ so that $M_1\odot L\odot M_2$ is defined,  and an endomorphism 
$Q\odot L\xrightarrow{f} L\odot P,$
let $M_1\odot f\odot M_2$ be the composite  
\begin{align*} 
 M_1\odot Q\odot N_1\odot M_1\odot L\odot M_2
 &\xrightarrow{\rsm{\epsilon}{M_1}{N_1}{Q} \odot \id_L \odot \id_{M_2}}
 M_1\odot Q\odot L\odot M_2
\\
 & \xrightarrow{\id_{M_1} \odot f\odot \id_{M_2}} M_1\odot L\odot P\odot M_2
\\
 &\xrightarrow{\id_{M_1}\odot \id_L\odot \rsm{\eta}{M_2}{N_2}{P}} M_1\odot L\odot M_2\odot N_2\odot P\odot M_2.
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: For $f: Q\odot L\to L\odot P$, $M_1\odot f\odot M_2$ composes $\epsilon$, $f$, and $\eta$ to a 2-cell between conjugated 1-cells.

nodes.name: Trace of conjugated 2-cell factors through tr(f)
nodes.statement: If $L$ is right dualizable \[\xymatrix@C=50pt{ \shvar{}{M_1\odot Q\odot N_1}\ar[r]^-{\mathrm{tr}(M_1\odot f\odot M_2)}\ar[d]_-{\mathrm{tr}\left( \rsm{\epsilon}{M_1}{N_1}{Q}\right)} &\shvar{}{N_2\odot P\odot M_2} \\ \shvar{}{Q}\ar[r]^-{\mathrm{tr}(f)}&\shvar{}{P}\ar[u]_{\mathrm{tr}\left( \rsm{\eta}{M_2}{N_2}{P}\right)} }\] commutes.
assumptions: If $L$ is right dualizable
nodes.statement_short: $\mathrm{tr}(M_1\odot f\odot M_2)$ equals $\mathrm{tr}(\eta)\circ\mathrm{tr}(f)\circ\mathrm{tr}(\epsilon)$.
nodes.label: euler_char_shadows_3

nodes.name: Proof of conjugated trace corollary
nodes.statement:
As the definition of $M_1\odot f\odot M_2$ suggests, 
this follows by applying 
\cref{lem:composite_dual_pair}
to the maps
\begin{gather*}
 M_1\odot Q\odot N_1\odot M_1\xrightarrow{\rsm{\epsilon}{M_1}{N_1}{Q}} M_1\odot Q
\\
Q\odot L \xrightarrow{ f} L\odot P
\\
P\odot M_2\xrightarrow{\rsm{\eta}{M_2}{N_2}{P}} M_2\odot N_2\odot P\odot M_2
\end{gather*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the composite-trace theorem to the three maps $\epsilon$, $f$, $\eta$.

nodes.name: Tightening for traces
nodes.statement: \cite[Prop.~7.1]{ps:bicat} Let $M$ be right dualizable, let $f \colon Q\odot M \to M \odot P$, $g\colon Q' \to Q$ and $h\colon P \to P'$ be 2-cells. Then \[ \shvar{}{h}\circ \mathrm{tr}(f)\circ\shvar{}{g}=\mathrm{tr} (\id_M \odot h)\circ f\circ (g\odot \id_M). \]
assumptions: Let $M$ be right dualizable, let $f \colon  Q\odot M \to M \odot P$, $g\colon  Q' \to Q$ and $h\colon P \to P'$ be 2-cells.
nodes.label: prop:tightening

nodes.name: Morita equivalence of 1-cells
nodes.statement: A pair of one cells $M\in \mc{B}(C,D)$ and $N\in \mc{B}(D,C)$ is a {\bf Morita equivalence} if $(M,N)$ and $(N,M)$ are dual pairs and the coevaluation and evaluation maps for each dual pair are inverses. That is, if $\eta_{(M,N)}$ and $\epsilon_{(M,N)}$ are the coevaluation and evaluation for $(M,N)$ and $\eta_{(N,M)}$ and $\epsilon_{(N,M)}$ are the coevaluation and evaluation for $(N,M)$ then \begin{align*} \eta_{(N,M)}\circ \epsilon_{(M,N)}=\id_{N\odot M} &\qquad \epsilon_{(N,M)}\circ \eta_{(M,N)}=\id_{U_{C}} \\ \eta_{(M,N)}\circ \epsilon_{(N,M)}=\id_{M\odot N}&\qquad \epsilon_{(M,N)}\circ \eta_{(N,M)}=\id_{U_{{D}}} \end{align*}
differentia: the coevaluation and evaluation maps for each dual pair are inverses
nodes.label: defn:morita_equivalence

nodes.name: Morita equivalent 0-cells
nodes.statement: If $M \in \mc{B}(C, D)$ and $N \in \mc{B}(D, C)$ define a Morita equivalence, then $C$ and $D$ are said to be \textbf{Morita equivalent}.

nodes.name: Dual pair subscripts
nodes.statement: Note that we use the dual pair as a subscript on the coevaluation and evaluation when there are multiple dual pairs. We will use a similar notation for the Euler characteristic.

nodes.name: Morita equivalence of rings
nodes.statement: In the bicategory of rings, bimodules, and homomorphisms, a Morita equivalence is a $(C,D)$-bimodule $M$ and a $(D,C)$-bimodule $N$ so that $(M,N)$ and $(N,M)$ are dual pairs and, using the coevaluation and evaluation from these dual pairs, \[ M\otimes_DN\cong C\qquad\text{and} \qquad N\otimes_CM\cong D. \] This is the familiar notion of Morita equivalence for rings and implies the functor \[ N\otimes_C- \colon \Mod_C\to \Mod_D \] is equivalence of the category of (left) modules over $C$ and the category of (left) modules over $D$. The most familiar example of Morita equivalence is that the ring of $n$-by-$n$ matrices with elements in $C$ is Morita equivalent to $C$ for any $n > 0$.

nodes.name: Euler characteristic of Morita equivalence is an isomorphism
nodes.statement: Suppose $(M,N)$ is a Morita equivalence. Then $\chi_{(M,N)}(M)=\chi_{(M,N)}(N)$ is an isomorphism with inverse $\chi_{(N,M)}(N)=\chi_{(N,M)}(M)$.
assumptions: Suppose  $(M,N)$ is a Morita equivalence.
nodes.label: euler_char_shadows

nodes.name: Proof Euler characteristic isomorphism
nodes.statement: \cref{fig:euler_char_compose} is a graphical representation of the composite of Euler characteristics where we have nested the red/green dual pair inside the orange/blue dual pair. Following \cref{fig:morita} we can first cancel the concentric green and orange regions resulting in \cref{fig:euler_char_compose_2}. Then the red and blue regions cancel. the commutative diagrams below are a more formal proof. \[\xymatrix@C=40pt{ \shvar{}{U_C}\ar[r]^-{\shvar{}{{\eta_{(M,N)}}}}\ar[rrrddd]^\id & \shvar{}{M\odot N}\ar[r]^\sim\ar[ddrr]^\id &\shvar{}{N\odot M}\ar[r]^-{\shvar{}{\epsilon_{(M,N)}}} \ar[dr]^\id &\shvar{}{U_D}\ar[d]^-{\shvar{}{{\eta_{(N,M)}}}} \\ \shvar{}{U_D}\ar[d]_-{\shvar{}{{\eta_{(N,M)}}}}\ar[ddrdrr]^\id &&&\shvar{}{N\odot M}\ar[d]^\sim \\ \shvar{}{N\odot M}\ar[d]^\sim\ar[ddrr]^\id &&&\shvar{}{M\odot N}\ar[d]^-{\shvar{}{\epsilon_{(N,M)}}} \\ \shvar{}{M\odot N}\ar[d]_-{\shvar{}{\epsilon_{(N,M)}}}\ar[dr]^\id &&&\shvar{}{U_C} \\ \shvar{}{U_C}\ar[r]_-{\shvar{}{{\eta_{(M,N)}}}} & \shvar{}{M\odot N}\ar[r]^\sim &\shvar{}{N\odot M}\ar[r]_-{\shvar{}{\epsilon_{(M,N)}}} &\shvar{}{U_D} }\]
nodes.statement_short: Nest the two dual pairs in a pasting diagram and cancel the inverse coevaluation/evaluation regions; formalized by commutative diagrams.

nodes.name: Nest dual pairs
nodes.statement: \cref{fig:euler_char_compose} is a graphical representation of the composite of Euler characteristics where we have nested the red/green dual pair inside the orange/blue dual pair.
nodes.statement_short: Represent the composite of Euler characteristics with nested dual pairs.

nodes.name: Cancel regions
nodes.statement: Following \cref{fig:morita} we can first cancel the concentric green and orange regions resulting in \cref{fig:euler_char_compose_2}. Then the red and blue regions cancel.
nodes.statement_short: Cancel green/orange then red/blue regions using the Morita relations.

nodes.name: Formal diagram
nodes.statement: the commutative diagrams below are a more formal proof. \[\xymatrix@C=40pt{ \shvar{}{U_C}\ar[r]^-{\shvar{}{{\eta_{(M,N)}}}}\ar[rrrddd]^\id & \shvar{}{M\odot N}\ar[r]^\sim\ar[ddrr]^\id &\shvar{}{N\odot M}\ar[r]^-{\shvar{}{\epsilon_{(M,N)}}} \ar[dr]^\id &\shvar{}{U_D}\ar[d]^-{\shvar{}{{\eta_{(N,M)}}}} \\ \shvar{}{U_D}\ar[d]_-{\shvar{}{{\eta_{(N,M)}}}}\ar[ddrdrr]^\id &&&\shvar{}{N\odot M}\ar[d]^\sim \\ \shvar{}{N\odot M}\ar[d]^\sim\ar[ddrr]^\id &&&\shvar{}{M\odot N}\ar[d]^-{\shvar{}{\epsilon_{(N,M)}}} \\ \shvar{}{M\odot N}\ar[d]_-{\shvar{}{\epsilon_{(N,M)}}}\ar[dr]^\id &&&\shvar{}{U_C} \\ \shvar{}{U_C}\ar[r]_-{\shvar{}{{\eta_{(M,N)}}}} & \shvar{}{M\odot N}\ar[r]^\sim &\shvar{}{N\odot M}\ar[r]_-{\shvar{}{\epsilon_{(M,N)}}} &\shvar{}{U_D} }\]
nodes.statement_short: Give the formal commutative diagram proof.

nodes.name: Trace of twisted coevaluation is an isomorphism
nodes.statement: Suppose $(M,N)$ is a Morita equivalence. If $Q$ is a 1-cell so that $N\odot Q\odot M$ is defined, \[ \shvar{}{Q} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{tr}\left(\rsm{\eta}{M}{N}{Q}\right)} \shvar{}{N\odot Q\odot M} \] is an isomorphism with inverse $\shvar{}{N\odot Q\odot M}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{tr}\left(\rsm{\epsilon}{N}{M}{Q}\right)} \shvar{}{Q} $.
assumptions: Suppose  $(M,N)$ is a Morita equivalence.
If $Q$ is a 1-cell so that $N\odot Q\odot M$ is defined

nodes.name: Proof twisted trace isomorphism

nodes.name: Morita invariance of THH
nodes.statement: Let $\mc{B}(\mathbf{Cat}(\operatorname{Sp}))$ be the bicategory of spectral categories (with the proper homotopy theoretic considerations, see \cref{bcat_example}) . Let $A$ be a ring spectrum. There are two spectral categories naturally associated with $A$ \begin{enumerate} \item The spectral category $\operatorname{Mod}^c_A$. \item The one object spectral category whose hom spectrum is $A$. We denote this category $\mathrm{End}_{ \operatorname{Mod}^c_A}(A)$ since it is the full subcategory of $\operatorname{Mod}^c_A$ with the single object $A$. \end{enumerate} There is an inclusion functor \[ E_A\colon \mathrm{End}_{ \operatorname{Mod}^c_A}(A) \to \Mod^c_A \] and so we can construct a 1-cell (i.e. a spectral bimodule) $ _{E_A} (\operatorname{Mod}^c_A)$. There is similarly a spectral bimodule $ (\Mod^c_A)_{E_A}$. These two bimodules are a Morita equivalence. Applying \cref{cor:base_change_morita_isos} with the substitutions \begin{center} \begin{tabular}{c|c|c} $\mc{A}$ & $\mc{C}$ & $F$\\\hline $\mathrm{End}_{\operatorname{Mod}^c_A} (A)$ & $\Mod^c_A$ & $E_A$ \end{tabular} \end{center} the map \begin{equation} \thh(A) \cong \thh\left(\mathrm{End}_{\Mod^c_A} (A)\right) \to \thh\left(\Mod^c_A\right) \end{equation} induced by the inclusion of $A$ into $\Mod^c_A$ as a module over itself is an isomorphism. We will give an explicit description of the inverse of this map on $\pi_0$ in \cref{lem:base_change_euler_inverse}.

Then $(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A)_{-\sma_AQ}$ is an $(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A, \operatorname{Mod}^c_A)$-bimodule and the inclusion \[ E_A\colon \mathrm{End}_{ \operatorname{Mod}^c_A}(A) \to \operatorname{Mod}^c_A \] defines a $(\mathrm{End}_{ \operatorname{Mod}^c_A}(A),\mathrm{End}_{ \operatorname{Mod}^c_A}(A))$-bimodule $_{E_A}((\operatorname{Mod}^c_A)_{-\sma_AQ})_{E_A}$. Since $E_A$ is a Morita equivalence, applying \cref{cor:base_change_morita_isos} with the substitutions \begin{center} \begin{tabular}{c|c|c|c} $\mc{A}$ &$\mc{C}$ &$F$ &$\mc{Q}$ \\ \hline $\mathrm{End}_{\operatorname{Mod}^c_A}(A)$ &$\operatorname{Mod}^c_A$ &$E_A$ &$(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A)_{-\sma_AQ}$ \end{tabular} \end{center} gives an isomorphism $\shvar{}{_{E_A}((\operatorname{Mod}^c_A)_{-\sma_AQ})_{E_A}} \to \shvar{}{(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A)_{-\sma_AQ}}$. nodes.name: Ring bimodule trace via functors
nodes.statement: We now return to the example at the beginning of this subsection. Let $C$ and $D$ be rings, $Q$ be an $(C,C)$-bimodule, $P$ be an $(D,D)$-bimodule, $M$ be an $(C,D)$-bimodule that is finitely generated and projective as an right $D$-module, and let $f\colon Q\otimes_C M\to M\otimes_D P$ be a homomorphism. \cref{ex:base_change_and_natural_transformation} with the substitutions \begin{center} \begin{tabular}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} $\mc{A}$ &$a$ &$\mc{C}$ &$c$ &$J$ &$K$ &$F$ &$\Phi$ \\ \hline $\Mod_C^c$ &$C$ &$\Mod_D^c$ &$D$ &${-\otimes_CQ}$ &${-\otimes_DP}$ &${-\otimes_CM}$ &$-\otimes_Cf$ \end{tabular} \end{center} implies the bottom square in the following diagram commutes. \[\xymatrix{ \shvar{}{Q} \ar[d] \ar[rr]^-{\mathrm{tr}(f)} &&\shvar{}{P}\ar[d] \\ \shvar{}{\Mod_C^c(C,Q)} \ar[d] \ar[rr]^-{\mathrm{tr}(f_*)} &&\shvar{}{\Mod_D^c(D,P)}\ar[d] \\ \shvar{}{(\Mod_C^c)_{-\otimes_CQ}}\ar[r]^-{\shvar{}{\psi}} &\shvar{}{_{-\otimes_CM}(\Mod_D^c)_{-\otimes_CM\otimes_DP}}\ar[r] &\shvar{}{(\Mod_D^c)_{-\otimes_DP}} }\] In this example, ${_{E_C}(\Mod_C^c)}\odot \phi\odot (\Mod_D^c)_{E_D}$ is \begin{align*} \Mod_C^c(C, Q)\odot \Mod_D^c(M,D) &\to \Mod_D^c(M, P) \\ (C\xrightarrow{\alpha} Q,M\xrightarrow{\beta}D) &\mapsto (C\otimes_CM\xrightarrow{\alpha\otimes\id}Q\otimes_AM\xrightarrow{ f}M\otimes _DP\xrightarrow{\beta\otimes \id}D\otimes_DP) \end{align*} The top square is the identification of $\Mod_C^c(C,Q)$ with $Q$ and $\Mod_D^c(D,P)$ with $P$ and the observation that the trace of the dual of a map is the trace of the map.

nodes.name: Restriction and transfer in THH
nodes.statement:
Let $R$ be a ring spectrum and $A$, $C$ be $R$-algebras.  A map of $R$-algebras $f\colon  A \to C$ defines an $(A, C)$-bimodule $_fC$.  If 
$_fC$
 is left dualizable, we have 
an adjunction
\[
 C_f \sma_A - \colon  \operatorname{Mod}^{lc}_{(A, R)} \leftrightarrows \operatorname{Mod}^{lc}_{(C, R)} \colon  \ _f C \sma_C - 
\]
between the bimodules that are left-compact (that is, for example, an $(A, R)$-bimodule is compact when considered as an $A$-module). Letting $R$ be the sphere spectrum and taking $\thh$ of both sides of the adjunction gives us maps
\[
\operatorname{res}\colon  \thh(\operatorname{Mod}^c_{A}) \leftrightarrows \thh(\operatorname{Mod}^c_C) \colon  \operatorname{trf} 
\]
which are usually referred to as \textbf{restriction} and \textbf{transfer}.
nodes.statement_short: An algebra map $f$ with ${}_fC$ dualizable gives an adjunction on compact modules; applying THH gives restriction and transfer maps.

nodes.name: Transfer-restriction is Euler characteristic
nodes.statement:
It is well know that the composite
\[
S \cong \thh(S) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{trf}} \thh(\Sigma^\infty_+ \Omega X) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{res} }  \thh (S) \simeq S 
\]
is the Euler characteristic.

nodes.name: Lind-Malkiewich and Becker-Gottlieb
nodes.statement: The above was proved in \cite{lind_malkiewich}, as a step in verifying the first-named author's conjecture that the Becker-Gottlieb transfer factors through the $\thh$ transfer.

nodes.name: Restriction-Transfer
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} \operatorname{res} \circ \operatorname{trf} = \chi(_fC_f) \colon \thh(A) \to \thh(A)\\ \operatorname{trf} \circ \operatorname{res} = \chi((C_f)\odot (_fC)) \colon \thh(C) \to \thh(C). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Restriction-transfer composites are Euler characteristics of composite base change bimodules.

nodes.name: Restriction-transfer examples
nodes.statement: We present two examples of these types of restriction-transfer identities \begin{itemize} \item Let $X$ be a path-connected space of the homotopy type of a finite CW-complex. If we let $A=S$ and $C=\Sigma^\infty_+ \Omega X$, then $A$ is compact as a $C$-module. The composite \[ S \simeq \thh (S) \xrightarrow{ \operatorname{trf}} \thh (\Sigma^\infty_+ \Omega X) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{res} } \thh (S) \simeq S \] is $\chi(X)$, regarded as an element of $\pi_0(S)$. \item Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$ where $[G:H] < \infty$. Then the base change object associated to the inclusion of the group ring $A = \mathbb{Z}[H]$ into $C = \mathbb{Z}[G]$ is dualizable. The shadow is $\operatorname{HH}_0 (\mathbb{Z}[G], \mathbb{Z}[G])$ and \[ \operatorname{HH}_0 (\mathbb{Z}[H],\mathbb{Z}[H]) \xrightarrow{ \operatorname{trf}} \operatorname{HH}_0 (\mathbb{Z}[G],\mathbb{Z}[G]) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{res} } \operatorname{HH}_0 (\mathbb{Z}[H], \mathbb{Z}[H]) \] is multiplication by $[G:H]$. This has an interpretation in terms of the character theory of group representations, since $\operatorname{HH}_0 (\mathbb{Z}[G], \mathbb{Z}[G]) \cong \mathbb{Z}[C_G]$ where $C_G$ denotes the conjugacy classes of $G$. Since maps from $\mathbb{Z}[C_G]$ are exactly class functions, this is the same $[G:H]$ that appears in the classical induction-restriction maps in character theory for representations of finite groups. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: For $S\to\Sigma^\infty_+\Omega X$ the composite is $\chi(X)$; for $\mathbb{Z}[H]\to\mathbb{Z}[G]$ it is multiplication by $[G:H]$.
